children: Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr expressed concern Tuesday that the country isn't properly prepared for AI-related disruptions to the labor market.

"The Federal Reserve and indeed the country are grappling what AI means," Barr said in Detroit. "In my judgment, now is the time for society to begin to consider how to address these potential disruptions."
Barr said he doesn't foresee much disruption to the workforce in the next year or so. "Across the economy there is little evidence yet of significant displacement so far," he said.

Goldman Sachs economist Elsie Peng has estimated that just a 0.10 percentage point drag on total unemployment last year was attributable to AI. And the unemployment rate has hovered near historic lows for the past few years, despite the introduction of AI.
The "greatest uncertainty" then is in the medium term, or roughly the next two to five years, Barr said.

This is because it's tricky to forecast right now exactly how and when productivity gains attributable to AI might take hold. If AI adoption and AI-related productivity gains show up faster than expected in that time frame, it may be hard for workers to adjust. In that case, "dislocation may be large," Barr added. A slower shift "might permit more orderly adjustments."

In the longer-term, how well the labor market weathers the AI revolution depends on whether there is adequate investment in creating new jobs, training workers, and connecting workers to new roles, he added.

If AI does indeed significantly boost productivity and the AI buildout remains robust, Barr said demand for capital will rise because of higher returns on investment. At the same time, household savings will fall as people expect higher real-wage growth. Barr said that combination will call for higher interest rates in equilibrium, meaning higher federal funds rates.
It is "too early to know" if that is happening yet, he said. Regardless, inflation is still too high.

Inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target since 2021. Core personal consumption expenditures, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.3% year over year in July, prompting the Federal Open Market Committee, which Barr is a voting member of, to increase its policy rate by 25 basis points this month.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh signaled multiple times after that rate increase that the FOMC is committed to "support a timelier return" to its inflation target. On Tuesday, Barr cast doubt on that path: "I don't see a clear trend to a timely return to 2%."
"I expect we will need further adjustments" to rates in 2027 to get there, he added.
